title: Lecture 6. Research in the prevention system
summary:
1 Why Research is Needed

2 Theoretical Model of Research

3 Main Research Methods in Behavioral Sciences

1. Why Research is Needed The methods of empirical research into social behavior are fundamentally natural science methods. Humans are studied as biological beings, representatives of a population. For example, in an unbalanced market, when studying consumer behavior regarding food products, the same methods are applied as when studying biological behavior, for instance, of a reindeer in conditions of lichen deficiency (social-marketing research). Initially, these methods found application and development in epidemiology. When studying the spread of infectious diseases, it was found that these diseases are transmitted in full accordance with social dynamics (population density, nature of contacts, communication channels, etc.). As early as the 19th century, it was recognized that the territorial spread of infectious diseases accurately reflects existing social structures and processes. By the 1930s, this approach became a powerful heuristic tool, widely used for analyzing socio-structural factors in the development of non-infectious diseases (oncological, tuberculosis, diabetes, myocardial infarction – considered psychosomatic at the time). The analysis of the spread of infectious diseases by socio-structural variables was called analytical epidemiology.

There are two types of empirical studies of behavioral parameters: 1. Theoretically oriented social research. Their goal is the quantitative determination and elucidation of relationships between categories within mid-range theoretical models. 2. Research oriented towards applied tasks. Their goal is to assess the adequacy and quantitatively determine the parameters of actually commonplace sociological theories. In other words, when we hear about research "without theory," it means that it is based on a pre-scientific, everyday theory. However, without a verbal description, i.e., explicitation, of such a pre-scientific theory, it is impossible to define a research program or prepare primary research documents. It must be emphasized that there is no research without underlying theoretical models, even if they are pre-scientific.

Research is necessary when there is a lack of essential information to achieve prevention goals. Three situations can be identified where research is used:

Within a prevention project at the stage of substantiating its goals and objectives; Within a prevention project at the stage of evaluating its results; Outside the scope of direct prevention work, when nevertheless systematic data collection and accumulation on a particular problem is required. Such data can be subject to secondary processing and used for prevention purposes by an indefinite circle of researchers and authors of various prevention projects. Examples of such research include monitoring studies in the field of youth psychological well-being: the Russian socio-psychological testing (SPT), the European ESPAD project, or the American "Monitoring the Future." A well-planned study takes less effort; it represents the same cultural value as a painting, a statue, or a film. Western studies in the main areas of sociology, conducted since the 1950s within modern methodology, are still in scientific circulation; their results are used, recalculated, and re-analyzed. For all fundamental social processes, there is a historical trend, meaning data obtained in the 1950s that cannot be obtained in the 1990s.

Research is a complex and expensive part of prevention work, so much so that there has long been a discussion among specialists about whether it is worth spending resources on it at all, or if it is sufficient to use intuitive ideas about the problem to engage in prevention. Research planning is the art of determining the optimal degree of required completeness and reliability of the results obtained, considering that any complication of the research plan inevitably entails additional financial and other costs. Therefore, when planning research, a formal procedure, described below, is followed.

2. Theoretical Model of Research At the foundation of any research lies a theoretical model, even when the authors of the research themselves do not realize it. And even in an ordinary everyday situation, when we, for example, ask in an unfamiliar city how to get to the library, we can identify the following elements of a theoretical model:

The problem to be solved — a contradiction between being at point A and needing to be at point B. The consequence of the problem — we are currently far from the library. The method of resolving the contradiction — obtaining information by asking passers-by. The sample (in this case, also the object) of the study — people who might know the way to the library. Moreover, intuitively, we will most likely choose to ask people who look like locals, not tourists. The main factor of our problem — our lack of knowledge about the library's location. The research hypothesis — that is, the connection between the factor and the problem to be solved: someone in our sample knows the correct way. In our simple case, this is also the subject of our research. The concepts listed above are elements of a theoretical model that can ALWAYS be identified in any research or prevention project. Graphically, the theoretical model of research can be represented as follows:

At the center of the figure is the problem to be solved. Below it are the factors that determine its state. And above are the consequences of the problem, what it manifests as, what we would like to eliminate. And the arrows — the connections between the problem, factors, and its consequences — are hypotheses, the strength of which any research tests.

Object – something physical, objectively existing, carrying a contradiction and generating a problematic situation (an individual, groups of people, communities). A study can include not one sample, but several; then all of them are the object of research.

Subject – the most significant properties of the object from theoretical and practical points of view, which most clearly reflect the contradictions we identify. Essentially, the subject is —

Factors and consequences that can be included in the study can be formulated as a result of a literature review on the topic, expert suggestions, or be contained in existing standardized scales.

The result of theoretical modeling of a study is a list of questions it must answer, also called programmatic questions. It is important to note that these are not questions from a questionnaire or a specific research method! These are questions for which adequate research procedures still need to be selected. Each study is built on a single list of programmatic questions, but many research methods can be used to collect information on them. Conclusions based on the research results are ultimately formulated using these same programmatic questions.

An example of programmatic questions for a study of drug use among adolescents might look like this (or differently, depending on the tasks set by the client, the specifics of the particular situation, and available resources for conducting the study):

Questions about Consequences
Seeking medical help
Problems with academic performance and school attendance
Police detentions related to drugs
Drug-related crimes
Problems in relationships with parents
Problems in relationships with peers
Problems in relationships with a romantic partner or in the family
QUESTIONS ABOUT THE PROBLEM
Significance of the drug addiction problem among other social problems in the region
Level and structure of drug use among youth in the region
Questions about factors

Causes of drug addiction spread; Factors promoting and hindering drug use; Drug availability, places of acquisition; Youth attitudes towards the problem of drug use; Age and circumstances of first drug use; Positive and negative motives and attitudes towards drug use

Note that questions about the problem (and there are usually few of them in a study) reflect the resulting variable of the theoretical model, while all other questions reflect factorial variables, i.e., those determining the state of the problem.

For example, when considering adolescent smoking, as resulting variables we could use types of cigarettes or smoking mixtures and frequency of smoking, and as factorial variables: circumstances of smoking — in groups or alone, where they buy cigarettes, with what funds, whether they want to quit smoking, how aware their parents and teachers are of adolescent smoking, what methods they use for smoking prevention, whether there are any norms regulating smoking in schools and other places, how students, their parents, and the administration of the educational institution relate to the possibility of implementing an anti-tobacco prevention program, etc.

The purpose of any research is to formulate and test hypotheses — that is, the strength of the connections between the resulting and factorial variables of the theoretical model. Without a theoretical model and the goal of testing specific hypotheses, research risks being useless. The only exception might be a research subject for which there is absolutely no preliminary information, and then the task is to obtain at least some primary data to build a model and conduct a full-fledged study later. But in the modern world, such a research subject is difficult to imagine.

3. Main Research Methods in Behavioral Sciences Below is a list of the main research methods used in behavioral sciences. The methods are ranked from the least formalized and individual at the bottom to the most formalized and mass at the top. The methodological basis of all research methods in behavioral sciences is the clinical interview. Other methods derive from it by formalizing certain elements of the basic research procedure.

It cannot be said that any of these methods is better or worse. In the following lessons of this module, the benefits and limitations of applying these methods, their applicability in various situations, and for prevention tasks will be discussed.

Socio-statistical research Sociological surveys, surveys of risk groups Psychological and socio-psychological tests Experiment Observation Semi-structured interview (individual, group, focus group) Clinical interview
